label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
# The Glenmore House

I'm going to say this once, properly, to everyone who reads this blog. Some of you have already heard bits of it on the phone, and that's my fault. I should have told you myself, and I should have started with the people closest to me. I'm sorry for how you found out. I'm not sorry for the decision itself, and I'll explain why below, as honestly as I can.

The house at Glenmore, out near Oughterard, is going to be sold. The sale was agreed on 3 November, and it closes on 15 January 2027. The buyers are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, and they have two small children. They want to live in the house, not rent it out as a holiday let, and they'll be moving in as a family, which is what the house was built for in the first place.

Most of you know the house as the Mulkerrin place, where Tom grew up. His grandfather Pádraig built it in 1931. Pádraig did the stonework himself, or so the story goes, and I've never been able to find out how much of that is true, because Tom told it differently every time. The house has been in the family for ninety-odd years. Tom died in March 2024, and since then I've been driving out there every second Saturday, forty minutes each way, to air the place and run the taps and make sure the pipes haven't frozen or burst. Some of you have asked me why I kept going out, and the honest answer is that I didn't know how to stop. Going out there was the only thing that made me feel he was still close by.

I want to explain how we got here, because I don't want anyone to think this was a sudden whim.

In September we had a roof survey done by Ó Flaithearta's. The slates on the main roof are going, and the back chimney needs to be taken down and rebuilt. The quote came to €38,000, and that's before the damp in the back bedroom is dealt with. The damp is coming from the wall where the old lean-to was, and it's the kind of problem that gets worse every winter you ignore it. The septic tank also has to be replaced before anyone can sell the house to anyone at all. None of that is news to people who know old houses, but it was news to me, and it was a hard thing to sit at the kitchen table in September and hear it all read out in one go.

I'm seventy-one. I was a primary-school teacher for thirty-four years, and I'm not used to being told I can't manage something. But I can't manage this. I tried to, for the best part of two years, and I've come to see that I was trying to keep the house so that I didn't have to face losing Tom. The house was never really about the building. It was about him.

Last February I slipped on the step at the back door. It had been frosty all night and I went out to check the pipes, which I always did, and my foot went from under me. I lay on the cold step for about twenty minutes before I could get up, and there was nobody to hear me. I got myself to the car and drove home very slowly. I didn't tell anybody. I didn't want the fuss, and I didn't want anyone telling me I shouldn't be going out there alone. I'm telling you now because it's part of why this has to happen, and because I'd rather you heard it from me.

Since the autumn I have been afraid of being alone out there. I don't mean afraid of the ghosts, though I suppose Tom would have had something to say about that. I mean that I'm afraid of falling again, and I'm afraid of how long it could be before somebody found me. I can't go on maintaining it, and I can't pretend that I can.

Now, Declan.

Declan, you heard about this from Gráinne on WhatsApp, not from me, and that is the thing I most regret. You had every right to hear it from your mother. You rang me at two in the morning your time, and you were upset, and you said I was selling Dad. I said things back that I shouldn't have said. I'm not going to repeat them here, because they were unkind and they weren't true, and I'm sorry for them. You're not a child, and you didn't deserve to be shouted at down a phone line in the middle of the night.

I also should have talked to you before I signed anything. I didn't, and I know that. I could give you reasons, about the timing and the roof and the way the offers came in over the summer, but none of that changes the fact that I should have sat down with you and said, this is what I'm thinking, what do you make of it. I regret not doing that. I'm not going to say that I'd do it differently in every way, because I'm not sure I would. The offer from the Joyces was lower than what some of the Dublin people put on the table in the summer. I took the lower one on purpose. Aoife and Kevin want the house to be a home, and I wanted someone who'd love it the way we did, not someone who'd sell it on in five years or let it to strangers for the summer. Tom would have wanted that. He always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum, and I don't think he'd have wanted it to sit empty and slowly fall down while we argued about it.

I'm not willing to wait until your summer visit. I know that's hard to hear. The roof won't wait, the damp won't wait, and I can't keep driving out there on my own. But I want you to know that I'm not angry with you. I'm not waiting for an apology, though I'm glad you've had the chance to tell me how you feel. The door is open. It was always open, and it still is.

Here's what's being kept, because I don't want anyone thinking we've thrown everything out.

The dresser is going to Úna. It's the big oak one from the kitchen, the one with the dent in the top where Tom dropped a crate of bottles in 1985, and it's far too heavy for anywhere I'm going, so it's going to the one person who'll polish it properly. Pádraig's fiddle is coming to me, and I'll be finding it a home with one of the grandchildren who'll actually learn to play it, not sit it in a corner. The photographs are all coming with me, every one of them, and I'll be scanning as many as I can so that the cousins in Boston and Perth and Leeds can have copies. The Sacred Heart lamp is staying in the hall with my mother's rosary beads hanging from it, and I'm not moving it. The gate sign, the one Tom painted that says MULKERRIN in letters that have faded to a sort of grey, is coming with me too.

The Joyces have been very generous. They've said that family can come out and walk the land any time, and I believe them. The fields down to the lake are still ours to walk, and the lake is still there to swim in. You all know the story about the children learning to swim there. Declan, you refused to come out of the water until your lips were blue, and Tom had to lift you onto the bank. I still think about that. I'm glad there are children going to be swimming in that lake again.

Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind the house in 1979. It was raining, and the cattle were all standing at the gate watching us like they had an opinion on it. He'd bought a ring in Galway that he couldn't afford, and he got down on one knee in the mud and I told him to get up before he ruined his good trousers. I said yes anyway. I think of that day more than I think of almost anything else in my life, and I'm not going to pretend I don't feel it now. I'm going to walk out to the haggard on the day out in December and stand exactly where he stood, and I'm going to let myself be sad about it, and then I'm going to come back in and have a cup of tea.

Over the best part of two years I've come to understand that I can keep Tom's memory without keeping the house. I didn't believe that for a long time. I thought the house was the memory. But the memory is in the photographs and the fiddle and the dresser and the lake and the gate sign, and in every one of you, and in the way you all still say "the Mulkerrin place" as if it's a country all its own. None of that needs a roof that doesn't leak.

So here is the day out.

Sunday 13 December, at Glenmore. We're going to have a family day before the house is cleared, and I want as many of you there as can make it. If you're in Galway, come out. If you're in Dublin, Boston, Perth or Leeds and you can't get over, we'll hold a space for you on the phone, and I'll have Úna set up a video call so you can walk round the rooms with us. Bring wellies, because the fields will be wet and the back path is worse than it looks. I'll have soup and sandwiches on the go all afternoon, and there's a flask of tea with your name on it. If you want to bring something for the table, bring it. If you want to bring a photograph of your own, bring that too. We'll have a box in the kitchen, and anything you want to leave there, you can.

Declan, I'd like you to come. I'd like you to walk down to the lake with me. You don't have to say anything. You don't have to forgive me before you get in the car. But I'd like to see you there, and I'd like us to stand in the haggard together and look at the place your father grew up, and to say goodbye to it the way we both should have been able to do.

If you're reading this and you're one of the cousins who heard about it on the grapevine, I'm sorry for that too. You're family, and you should have been told by me first. From now on I'll answer every question you have, whether on the phone or in the comments below, and I'll tell you the truth even when it's hard.

The sale closes on 15 January 2027. Between now and then, there's a lot to do: clearing the attic, sorting the outhouse, finding homes for the things that won't fit anywhere, and getting the photographs scanned before the boxes go. I'll post updates here as things happen, so that nobody has to hear it from someone else again.

Thank you for reading all the way to the end. I know it's a long post. I wanted to say it all in one place so that nobody had to put the pieces together from fragments.

Love to you all,

[Your name]
